Guidelines summarize and evaluate available evidence to assist health professionals in proposing the best management strategies for individual patients. They are not a substitute for the patient–practitioner relationship; final decisions must be made by responsible health professionals in consultation with patients and caregivers. The ESC makes its Guidelines freely available, warns that technical language may be misinterpreted, and declines responsibility for misinterpretation. Recent ESC guidelines include quality criteria for transparency; recommendations are available on the ESC website, and the Guidelines represent the official position of the ESC on a given topic and are regularly updated.

5.2.2. Primary prevention of radiation-induced cardiovascular toxicity
content.narrative_summary: The page discusses primary prevention of cancer therapy-related cardiovascular (CV) toxicity. It emphasizes managing dyslipidaemia and underlying CVD per 2021 ESC Guidelines, close monitoring of CV side effects, correcting electrolyte imbalances, and coordinating a multidisciplinary team (MDT) approach. For anthracycline chemotherapy, neurohormonal therapies (e.g., renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system blockers, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists) have reduced LVEF decline but require further large RCTs; dexrazoxane and liposomal anthracyclines are approved options for high CV risk or high cumulative doses, with specific dosing ratios recommended. For radiation therapy, advanced techniques (intensity-modulated RT, respiratory gating, proton therapy) minimize mean heart dose, though complete cardiac avoidance may be infeasible for certain tumour locations; MDT assessment of risk/benefit is advised and no proven medical therapies exist to prevent RT-induced CV toxicity, so tight control of CV risk factors is recommended.

content.narrative_summary: Section 5.5.1 describes anthracycline-induced CTRCD as a dose-dependent and cumulative process that may be symptomatic or asymptomatic. It introduces risk-based personalized monitoring protocols combining clinical assessment, transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), cardiac biomarkers (cTn and NP), 3D-LVEF and GLS, with references to recent position statements and guideline-based therapy for patients with pre-existing CVD. Section 5.5.2 outlines HER2-targeted therapies in early and metastatic breast cancer, approved agents (trastuzumab, pertuzumab, etc.), and recommends surveillance of LV function by LVEF and GLS prior to and every 3 months during treatment; it notes the limited validation of serum biomarkers (cTn, NP) in this context.

content.narrative_summary: This text continues discussion of surveillance and risk management in multiple myeloma (MM) patients. Monitoring of natriuretic peptides (NP) and cardiac troponin (cTn) with echocardiography during proteasome inhibitor (PI) therapy aids risk stratification and cardiovascular morbidity management. Hypertension may contribute to HFpEF. MM patients have elevated thrombosis risk due to patient- and myeloma-related factors, especially when combining PI and immunomodulatory drugs (IMiDs). In the ASPIRE trial, adding carfilzomib to lenalidomide and dexamethasone increased VTE rates (6.6% vs 3.9%). Oncology guidelines recommend aspirin or prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) for low-risk patients on thalidomide- or lenalidomide-based regimens and therapeutic LMWH for high-risk patients. Emerging small studies suggest low-dose apixaban and rivaroxaban are effective and safe for VTE prevention, but larger trials are needed.

section_headings: 5.5.8. Rapidly accelerated fibrosarcoma and mitogen-activated extracellular signal-regulated kinase inhibitor treatment
content.narrative_summary: RAF inhibitors (vemurafenib, dabrafenib, encorafenib) are approved for metastatic melanoma with a BRAF V600 mutation, and MEK inhibitors (trametinib, cobimetinib, binimetinib, selumetinib) show activity in BRAF-mutated tumours. Key cardiovascular effects include hypertension, pulmonary embolism, cancer therapy–related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD), and QTc prolongation (particularly with cobimetinib plus vemurafenib). RAF inhibitors alone or combined with MEK inhibitors increase risk of myocardial infarction and atrial fibrillation. Patients with pre-existing cardiovascular disease have higher adverse event rates during MEK/RAF therapy, so baseline risk stratification is recommended. MEK inhibitors account for most cardiotoxicity, augmented by RAF inhibitor coadministration. CTRCD can appear from one month to two years post therapy; baseline echocardiography is advised for moderate–high risk patients. During treatment, monitor blood pressure at each visit with weekly outpatient checks for three months then monthly thereafter. For cobimetinib/vemurafenib, obtain ECG at 2 and 4 weeks and every three months. In high-risk patients, consider echocardiographic surveillance of ventricular function every 6–12 months. Cardioprotective agents such as ACE inhibitors and ARBs may be used.

content.narrative_summary: CAR-T therapy for acute lymphocytic leukaemia and aggressive B-cell lymphomas is increasingly recognised to cause cardiovascular toxicities (CTR-CVT), including left ventricular dysfunction, heart failure, arrhythmias, pericardial effusion, stress cardiomyopathy, and cardiac arrest. Baseline cardiovascular evaluation (ECG, natriuretic peptides, and cardiac troponin) is recommended for all patients, with transthoracic echocardiography in those with pre-existing cardiovascular risk or disease. Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) can present with fever, tachypnoea, hypotension, tachycardia, hypoxia, and end-organ dysfunction, warranting a high index of suspicion. In adults, CRS severity correlates with cTn elevations and subsequent CV events. Retrospective data show CAR-T is associated with tachyarrhythmias (especially atrial fibrillation), ventricular arrhythmias, cardiomyopathy, and pleuro-pericardial disease, with a global CV/pulmonary adverse event fatality rate of ~30.9%. Early post-CAR-T evaluation should include natriuretic peptides, ECG, and echocardiography (see Section 6.1.4). Adoptive TIL therapy in metastatic melanoma also carries myocardial and vascular toxicity, with baseline and surveillance pathways mirroring those for CAR-T.

content.narrative_summary: The text discusses anticoagulation strategies in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) and cancer. It notes that low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) efficacy for stroke or systemic embolism prevention in AF has not been established and is based on evidence from venous thromboembolism (VTE). NOAC use in cancer patients is limited by drug–drug interactions, renal dysfunction, bleeding risk in gastrointestinal or genitourinary malignancies, and impaired absorption. section_headings: 6.4.2. Long corrected QT interval and ventricular arrhythmias
content.narrative_summary: Ventricular arrhythmias (VA) are uncommon during cancer but increase with advanced disease and cardiovascular comorbidities. Proposed mechanisms include direct effects of cancer drugs on ion‐channel expression and arrhythmogenic substrates from inflammation and pre‐existing comorbidities. Management follows general clinical guidelines: asymptomatic self‐terminating VA may not require drug discontinuation unless additional QT‐related risk factors or ECG abnormalities persist; symptomatic VA warrants dose reduction or discontinuation and cardiology referral. Life‐threatening VA requires urgent intervention. Beta-blockers and class IB agents are preferred to avoid drug–drug interactions and QT prolongation; amiodarone is recommended in patients with structural heart disease and hemodynamic instability.

content.title: 6.6. Thrombosis and thromboembolic events
content.narrative_summary: The section introduces cancer-associated thrombosis, defining arterial and venous thromboembolism in malignancy, noting VTE as the second-leading cause of death in cancer patients. Cancer increases VTE risk fivefold, especially around diagnosis, hospitalization, chemotherapy, and with metastatic disease. Unprovoked VTE may signal malignancy, and screening with lower-extremity ultrasonography or contrast-enhanced CT is recommended per 2019 ESC pulmonary embolism guidelines.

content.narrative_summary: Section 6.6.2 discusses that cancer confers a two‐fold higher risk of arterial thromboembolism (ATE)—including myocardial infarction and ischaemic stroke—with higher risk in men, older patients, and those with lung or kidney cancer. Pathophysiology includes tumour-induced carotid artery disease, tumour cell emboli, non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, paradoxical cerebral embolism, and cerebral sinus thrombosis. Section 6.6.3 explains that intracardiac thrombi in patients with malignancy arise from prothrombotic properties of cancer, its treatment, and central venous catheter use. Thrombus is most commonly intracardiac and may occur in any chamber; right atrial thrombi often relate to catheter malposition. Intraventricular thrombi occur in cancer therapy–related cardiac dysfunction, and left atrial appendage thrombi associate with atrial fibrillation or cancer therapy. Patients with systemic embolization should be screened with transthoracic or transoesophageal echocardiography, with cardiac MRI more sensitive and specific than TTE.

content.narrative_summary: Bleeding complications are more common in patients with cancer than in those without, due to tumour effects or chemotherapy/RT-induced mucosal weakening. GI and GU cancers pose high bleeding risk, exacerbated by thrombocytopaenia, platelet dysfunction, bone marrow suppression, age, renal/hepatic impairment, metastatic disease, low body mass index, and certain therapies (ibrutinib, VEGFi, cetuximab, bevacizumab). Proton pump inhibitors should be routine. Antiplatelet therapy, especially DAPT after ACS/PCI, increases bleeding ~1.6-fold; risk is highest within one year of cancer diagnosis. To minimize bleeding, DAPT duration/intensity should be limited, triple therapy avoided, thresholds for platelet counts set for initiation (≥10 000/µL for CV, ≥30 000/µL for DAPT), clopidogrel preferred if <50 000/µL, radial PCI approach preferred, and prophylactic platelet transfusions considered if <20 000/µL. Management includes controlling bleeding source, platelet transfusions for thrombocytopaenia, withholding/reversing anticoagulation for life-threatening bleeds, considering antifibrinolytics, supporting haemostasis, and avoiding recombinant factor VII or prothrombin concentrates in recent thrombosis.

content.narrative_summary: Pericardial diseases in cancer patients may result from various antineoplastic therapies and require differentiation from other causes. Diagnosis relies on history, examination, and imaging modalities (TTE, CT, CMR). Pericarditis follows similar criteria as non-cancer patients but may be atypical; acute radiation-induced cases are usually self-limiting, and ICI-related pericarditis often occurs around 30 days after therapy, with treatment including anti-inflammatories, corticosteroids, pericardiocentesis and ICI interruption based on severity. Pericardial effusions occur in <30% of cancer patients and up to 30% of malignant cases present as tamponade; small-to-medium effusions can be monitored, while large or symptomatic effusions often require percutaneous pericardiocentesis, intrapericardial therapies, or surgical pericardial window to prevent recurrence and tamponade.

content.narrative_summary: Valvular heart disease (VHD) can develop in cancer survivors typically 10 or more years after chest radiotherapy, causing stenosis or regurgitation, with up to 40% incidence after high-dose RT but <10% clinically significant. Management depends on severity and risk, with transcatheter (TAVI) or surgical valve interventions considered at intermediate risk and multidisciplinary Heart Team evaluation recommended. Peripheral artery and cerebrovascular disease may arise before, during, or after cancer therapy due to agents like cisplatin, BCR-ABL inhibitors, and radiotherapy, leading to accelerated vascular aging, inflammation, and significant carotid or peripheral arterial stenoses; vascular risk reduction should follow standard CVD prevention guidelines. Pericardial complications include acute pericarditis from anthracyclines and chronic constrictive pericarditis decades after RT; surveillance with echocardiography may be considered, but incidence, timing, and protocols remain uncertain.

content.narrative_summary: Following recommendations for pregnant women with cancer, the text discusses management of carcinoid valvular heart disease. It notes that somatostatin analogues (e.g. octreotide) should be administered peri-procedurally to avoid carcinoid crisis, with an infusion started up to 12 h pre-operatively and continued for at least 48 h post-valve surgery. Baseline and serial ECGs are recommended in patients at risk of QTc prolongation during ADT therapy.
Annual CV risk assessment is recommended during ADT.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 17 for baseline risk assessment and monitoring during endocrine therapy for breast cancer

rows.recommendation: Baseline CV risk assessment and estimation of 10-year fatal and non-fatal CVD risk with SCORE2 or SCORE2-OP is recommended in BC patients receiving endocrine therapies without pre-existing CVD.
Annual CV risk assessment is recommended during endocrine therapy in BC patients with high 10-year risk of (fatal and non-fatal) CV events according to SCORE2/SCORE2-OP.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 18 for baseline risk assessment and monitoring during cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 inhibitor therapy

rows.recommendation: QTc monitoring is recommended at baseline and 14 and 28 days in all patients with cancer receiving ribociclib.
QTc monitoring is recommended in patients treated with ribociclib with any dose increase.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 19 for baseline risk assessment and monitoring during ALK and EGFR inhibitors

rows.recommendation: Baseline CV risk assessment is recommended in patients before ALK inhibitors and EGFR inhibitors.
Baseline echocardiography is recommended in all patients with cancer before starting osimertinib.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 20 for baseline risk assessment and monitoring in patients receiving chimeric antigen receptor T cell and tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes therapies

rows.recommendation: Baseline ECG, NP, and cTn are recommended in all patients with cancer before starting CAR-T and TIL therapies.
A baseline echocardiography is recommended in patients with pre-existing CVD before starting CAR-T and TIL therapies.
Measurement of NP, cTn, and echocardiography are recommended in patients who develop CRS of ASTCT ≥ 2.

rows.recommendation: Baseline CV risk assessment and estimation of 10-year fatal and non-fatal CVD risk with SCORE2 or SCORE2-OP is recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 22 for baseline risk assessment in haematopoietic stem cell transplantation patients

rows.recommendation: Baseline and serial CV risk assessment (3 and 12 months, then yearly) including BP measurement, ECG, lipid measurement, and HbA1c is recommended in HSCT patients.
Echocardiography is recommended in all patients before HSCT.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 23 for the management of cardiovascular disease and cancer therapy-related cardiovascular toxicity in patients receiving anticancer treatment

rows.recommendation: A specialist CV assessment is recommended for optimal diagnostic workup and management of patients with cancer who present with new CV toxicity during and after cancer treatment.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 24 for the management of cancer treatment-related cardiac dysfunction during anthracycline chemotherapy

rows.recommendation: HF therapy is recommended for patients who develop symptomatic CTRCD during anthracycline chemotherapy.
Discontinuation of anthracycline chemotherapy is recommended in patients who develop symptomatic severe CTRCD.

Temporary interruption of anthracycline chemotherapy is recommended in patients who develop symptomatic moderate CTRCD and a multidisciplinary approach regarding the decision to restart is recommended.
A multidisciplinary approach regarding interruption vs. continuation of anthracycline chemotherapy is recommended in patients who develop mild symptomatic CTRCD.
Temporary interruption of anthracycline chemotherapy and initiation of HF therapy is recommended in patients who develop asymptomatic moderate or severe CTRCD.
A multidisciplinary approach regarding the decision when to restart is recommended in all patients with moderate or severe asymptomatic CTRCD.
Continuation of anthracycline chemotherapy is recommended in asymptomatic patients who have LVEF ≥ 50% and who have developed a significant fall in GLS or a troponin or a NP elevation > ULN.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 25 for the management of cancer treatment-related cardiac dysfunction during HER2-targeted therapies

rows.recommendation: HF therapy is recommended for patients who develop symptomatic moderate-to-severe CTRCD with LVEF < 50% during HER2-targeted treatment.

Temporary interruption of HER2-targeted treatment is recommended in patients who develop moderate or severe symptomatic CTRCD and the decision to restart should be based on a multidisciplinary approach after improvement of LV function and symptoms resolved.
In patients who develop mild symptomatic CTRCD, HF therapy and a multidisciplinary approach regarding the decision to continue vs. interrupt HER2-targeted therapy are recommended.
Temporary interruption of HER2-targeted therapy and initiation of HF therapy is recommended in patients who develop asymptomatic severe CTRCD.
A multidisciplinary approach regarding the decision to restart HER2-targeted treatment is recommended in patients with severe asymptomatic CTRCD.
Continuation of HER2-targeted therapy is recommended in patients who develop asymptomatic mild (LVEF ≥ 50%) CTRCD with more frequent cardiac monitoring.
ACE-I/ARB and beta-blockers are recommended in patients who develop asymptomatic moderate (LVEF 40–49%) CTRCD during HER2-targeted treatment.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 26 for the diagnosis and management of immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated myocarditis

rows.recommendation: cTn, ECG, and CV imaging (echocardiography and CMR) are recommended to diagnose ICI-associated myocarditis.
In patients with suspected ICI-associated myocarditis, temporary interruption of ICI treatment is recommended until the diagnosis is confirmed or refuted.

rows.recommendation: Interruption of ICI treatment is recommended in patients with confirmed ICI-associated myocarditis.
Continuous ECG monitoring to assess for new AV block and tachyarrhythmias during the acute phase is recommended for all patients with symptomatic ICI-associated myocarditis.
Early high-dose corticosteroids are recommended in patients with cancer and confirmed ICI-associated myocarditis.

Continuation of high-dose corticosteroids is recommended for the treatment of ICI-associated myocarditis until resolution of symptoms, LV systolic dysfunction, conduction abnormalities, and significant cTn reduction.

Admission to ICU (level 3), treatment with i.v. methylprednisolone, and optimal CV treatment including mechanical support (when indicated) is recommended for patients with ICI-associated fulminant myocarditis.
A multidisciplinary discussion is recommended before restarting ICI treatment in selected patients with previous uncomplicated ICI-associated myocarditis.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 27 for the diagnosis and management of Takotsubo syndrome in patients with cancer

rows.recommendation: Coronary angiography (invasive or CCTA) is recommended to exclude ACS.
CMR is recommended to exclude myocarditis and MI.
QT-prolonging drugs are not recommended during the acute TTS phase.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 28 for the management of acute coronary syndromes in patients receiving anticancer treatment

rows.recommendation: An invasive strategy is recommended in patients with cancer presenting with STEMI or high-risk NSTE-ACS with life expectancy ≥6 months.
A temporary interruption of cancer therapy is recommended in patients where the cancer therapy is suspected as a contributing cause.
In patients with cancer, thrombocytopaenia and ACS, aspirin is not recommended if platelets <10 000/µL.
In patients with cancer, thrombocytopaenia and ACS, clopidogrel is not recommended if platelets <30 000/µL and prasugrel or ticagrelor are not recommended if platelets <50 000/µL.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 29 for the management of chronic coronary syndromes in patients receiving anticancer treatment

rows.recommendation: Individualized duration of DAPT is recommended in patients with cancer with CCS, following revascularization, based upon thrombotic/ischaemic and bleeding risk, type and stage of cancer, and current cancer treatment.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 30 for the management of valvular heart disease in patients receiving anticancer treatment

rows.recommendation: In patients with cancer and pre-existing severe VHD, management according to the 2021 ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the management of VHD is recommended, taking into consideration cancer prognosis and patient preferences.

In patients with cancer developing new VHD during cancer therapy, management according to the 2021 ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the management of VHD is recommended, taking into consideration cancer prognosis and patient comorbidities.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 31 for the management of atrial fibrillation in patients receiving anticancer treatment

rows.recommendation: Long-term anticoagulation is recommended for stroke/systemic thromboembolism prevention in patients with cancer with AF and a CHA2DS2-VASc score ≥2 (men) or ≥3 (women) as per the 2020 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of atrial fibrillation.
Thromboembolic and bleeding risk reassessment is recommended during follow-up in patients with cancer with AF.
Antiplatelet therapy or prophylactic LMWH are not recommended for stroke or systemic thromboembolism prevention in AF with cancer.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 32 for the management of long QTc and ventricular arrhythmias in patients receiving anticancer treatment

rows.recommendation: Discontinuation of QTc-prolonging cancer therapy is recommended in patients who develop TdP or sustained ventricular tachyarrhythmias during treatment.

Temporary interruption of QTc-prolonging cancer therapy is recommended in patients who develop asymptomatic QTcF ≥500 ms and an ECG should be repeated every 24 h until resolution of the QTcF prolongation.
Immediate withdrawal of any offending drug and correction of electrolyte abnormalities and other risk factors is recommended in patients with cancer who develop QTcF ≥500 ms.
Weekly ECG monitoring is recommended in asymptomatic patients with cancer with QTcF 480–500 ms who are treated with a QTc-prolonging cancer therapy.

content.narrative_summary: This page continues guideline recommendations covering ECG monitoring after QTc-prolonging cancer therapy dose increases; criteria and procedures for restarting QTc-prolonging drugs; blood pressure targets and antihypertensive therapy in cancer patients; treatment and prophylaxis of venous thromboembolism including catheter-associated VTE; management of peripheral artery disease, pulmonary hypertension, and acute pericardial disease in patients undergoing anticancer treatment.

recommendation_tables.title: QTc-prolonging cancer therapy

rows.recommendation: A 12-lead ECG is recommended after any dose increase of QTc-prolonging cancer therapy.
A multidisciplinary discussion is recommended before restarting QTc-prolonging drugs in patients who have developed significant QTcF prolongation, to discuss alternative cancer treatments.
Weekly ECG monitoring during the first 4–6 weeks and then monthly thereafter is recommended in patients with cancer after restarting QTc-prolonging cancer therapy.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 33 for the management of arterial hypertension in patients receiving anticancer treatment

rows.recommendation: Effective treatment of cancer therapy-induced arterial hypertension to prevent cancer treatment interruption and CV complications is recommended.
A BP target <140 mmHg systolic and <90 mmHg diastolic is recommended during cancer therapy.

The competing cancer and CV risk evaluation is recommended if the systolic BP is ≥180 mmHg or diastolic BP ≥110 mmHg, and any cancer therapy associated with hypertension should be deferred or temporarily withheld until the BP is controlled to values <160 mmHg (systolic) and <100 mmHg (diastolic).
ACE-I or ARB are the first-line antihypertensive drugs recommended for BP management in patients with cancer.
Dihydropyridine CCB are recommended as second-line antihypertensive drugs for patients with cancer with uncontrolled BP.
Combination therapy with ACE-I or ARB and dihydropyridine CCB is recommended in patients with cancer with systolic BP ≥160 mmHg and diastolic BP ≥100 mmHg.
Diltiazem and verapamil are not recommended to treat arterial hypertension in patients with cancer due to their drug–drug interactions.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 34 for the management of venous thromboembolism in patients receiving anticancer treatment

rows.recommendation: Apixaban, edoxaban, or rivaroxaban are recommended for the treatment of symptomatic or incidental VTE in patients with cancer without contraindications.
LMWH are recommended for the treatment of symptomatic or incidental VTE in patients with cancer with platelet count >50 000 /µL.
Duration of anticoagulation in patients with cancer with a catheter-associated VTE is recommended for a minimum of 3 months and continuing longer if the catheter remains in situ.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 35 for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis during anticancer treatment

rows.recommendation: Extended prophylaxis with LMWH for 4 weeks post-operatively is recommended for patients with cancer undergoing major open or laparoscopic abdominal or pelvic surgery with low bleeding risk and high VTE risk.

Prophylactic LMWH for the primary prevention of VTE is indicated in hospitalized patients with cancer or those with prolonged bed rest or reduced mobility in the absence of bleeding or other contraindications.

A discussion with the patient about the relative benefits and harms, cancer prognosis, drug cost, and duration of treatment is recommended prior to prophylactic anticoagulation for the primary prevention of VTE.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 36 for management of peripheral artery disease during anticancer treatment

rows.recommendation: In patients who develop new symptomatic PAD, a multidisciplinary approach regarding the decision to continue vs. interrupt culprit cancer therapy is recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 37 for the management of pulmonary hypertension during anticancer treatment

rows.recommendation: Right-heart catheterization and discontinuation of dasatinib is recommended in patients who develop symptomatic or asymptomatic increase in peak TRV > 3.4 m/s.
In patients with confirmed dasatinib-induced PAH or new asymptomatic peak TRV > 3.4 m/s, an alternative BCR-ABL inhibitor is recommended after peak TRV recovery to < 2.8 m/s.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 38 for the management of pericardial diseases in patients receiving anticancer treatment

rows.recommendation: Diagnosis and management of acute pericarditis in patients with cancer based on the 2015 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases is recommended and a multidisciplinary discussion is needed before interrupting cancer therapy.

content.narrative_summary: This page presents a series of recommendation tables on the diagnosis and management of ICI-associated pericarditis, end-of-cancer-therapy cardiovascular risk assessment, and cardiovascular surveillance strategies for various adult cancer survivor populations, including those with childhood exposures and therapy-related cardiac dysfunction.

recommendation_tables.title: Diagnosis and management of ICI-associated pericarditis

rows.recommendation: Multimodality CV imaging (echocardiography, CMR ± CT), ECG and measurement of cardiac biomarkers are recommended to confirm the diagnosis, assess the haemodynamic consequences of pericardial disease, and rule out associated myocarditis.
Prednisolone and colchicine are recommended for patients with ICI-associated pericarditis.
Interruption of ICI treatment in patients with confirmed ICI-associated pericarditis with moderate-to-severe pericardial effusion is recommended.
A multidisciplinary discussion is recommended before restarting ICI treatment.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 39 for end-of-cancer therapy cardiovascular risk assessment

rows.recommendation: Educating and supporting patients with cancer to make appropriate healthy lifestyle choices is recommended.
Education is recommended for patients with cancer regarding recognition for early signs and symptoms of CVD.
CVRF assessment is recommended during the first year after cancer therapy and thereafter according to the 2021 ESC Guidelines on CVD prevention in clinical practice.
In asymptomatic high-risk patients, echocardiography and cardiac serum biomarkers are recommended at 3 and 12 months after completion of cancer therapy.

Cardiology referral is recommended in patients with cancer with new cardiac symptoms or new asymptomatic abnormalities in echocardiography and/or cardiac serum biomarkers at the end of therapy assessment.
Long-term continuation of cardiac medication is recommended in patients who develop severe CTRCD during cancer therapy.
CV follow-up and treatment optimization is recommended in patients who developed TKI-mediated hypertension during cancer therapy.
CV follow-up and treatment optimization is recommended in patients who developed vascular toxicities during cancer therapy.
ECG follow-up is recommended in patients who developed QT lengthening or LQTS during cancer therapy.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 40 for cardiovascular surveillance in asymptomatic adults who are childhood and adolescent cancer survivors

rows.recommendation: Education of adults who are childhood and adolescent CS treated with anthracyclines, mitoxantrone, and/or RT to a volume including the heart and their healthcare providers regarding their increased CV risk is recommended.
Annual screening for modifiable CVRF is recommended in adults who are childhood and adolescent CS treated with anthracyclines, mitoxantrone, and/or RT to a volume including the heart.
CV assessment is recommended in female childhood and adolescent CS prior to pregnancy or in the first trimester.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 41 for cardiovascular surveillance in asymptomatic adult cancer survivors

rows.recommendation: Annual CV risk assessment, including ECG and NP, and CVRF management is recommended in CS who were treated with a potentially cardiotoxic cancer drug or RT.
CV toxicity risk stratification is recommended 5 years after therapy to organize long-term follow-up.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 42 for adult cancer survivors who develop cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction late after cardiotoxic cancer therapy

rows.recommendation: ACE-I/ARB and/or beta-blockers are recommended in adult CS with moderate asymptomatic CTRCD.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 43 for adult cancer survivors with coronary artery disease

rows.recommendation: Non-invasive stress testing is recommended in asymptomatic CS with new moderate or severe radiation-induced CAD detected on CCTA to guide ischaemia-directed management.
A MDT discussion is recommended for clinical decision-making in patients with radiation-induced CAD and inducible ischaemia or severe left main CAD.

recommendation_tables.title: Symptomatic CAD

rows.recommendation: Pre-operative assessment of LIMA and RIMA viability, venous access, and sternal wound healing is recommended in CS with radiation-induced CAD where CABG is considered.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 44 for adult cancer survivors with valvular heart disease

rows.recommendation: A MDT approach is recommended to discuss and define the surgical risk in CS with severe VHD.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 46 for cardiovascular monitoring in cancer survivors during pregnancy

rows.recommendation: In high-risk female CS, pre-pregnancy counselling and management during pregnancy and around delivery by a multidisciplinary pregnancy heart team is recommended.
A baseline CV evaluation including history, physical examination, ECG, NP, and echocardiography is recommended in female CS with a history of CTRCD who are considering pregnancy.

A CV evaluation including echocardiography is recommended at 12 weeks of pregnancy in female CS who are either high-risk or who received potentially cardiotoxic cancer therapy and did not have a baseline CV assessment.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 47 for cardiovascular assessment and monitoring of pregnant women with cancer

rows.recommendation: Management by an expert MDT (the pregnancy heart team) in an expert centre is recommended for pregnant women with cancer who require cardiotoxic cancer therapy.
Cardiac assessment prior to cardiotoxic cancer therapy in pregnant women is recommended and consists of clinical history, physical examination, ECG, and echocardiography.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 48 for carcinoid valvular heart diseases

rows.recommendation: Echocardiography is recommended for the detection of carcinoid cardiac involvement in all patients with carcinoid syndrome and elevated NP levels and/or clinical signs of carcinoid heart disease, and for surveillance every 3 or 6 months depending on the severity of cardiac involvement and clinical status.
A MDT discussion for optimal medial management to prevent carcinoid crisis is recommended before any invasive or surgical cardiac procedure.
Valve replacement surgery is recommended in symptomatic patients with severe carcinoid tricuspid or pulmonary VHD and an expected survival ≥12 months.
Valve replacement or repair surgery is recommended in symptomatic patients with severe carcinoid mitral or aortic VHD and an expected survival ≥12 months.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 49 for amyloid light-chain cardiac amyloidosis diagnosis and monitoring

rows.recommendation: Echocardiography, NP, and cTn are recommended for the diagnosis of AL-CA in patients with plasma cell dyscrasia.
CMR is recommended in patients with suspected AL-CA.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 50 for risk stratification and monitoring for patients with cardiac implantable electronic devices undergoing radiotherapy

rows.recommendation: Risk stratification including planned radiation type and energy, dose to CIED, the patient’s device type, and pacing dependence is recommended prior to starting treatment.
In patients undergoing RT, a CIED check is recommended in all patients before and after completing RT, and during RT according to individual risk.
In patients with a CIED undergoing RT at high risk of arrhythmia and/or device dysfunction, ECG monitoring and/or pulse oximetry are recommended during every RT session.
